To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) signage interventions for stair use at work have inconsistent effects on stair use; (2) signage interventions have a small effect on stair use compared to pedestrian movement at the choice point; (3) signage interventions have inconsistent effects on the health behavior of interest, stair climbing, compared to stair descent; and (4) signage interventions are not an effective tool to improve population stair use.

1) signage interventions for stair use in the workplace may be effective but the evidence is weak and 2) the effectiveness of these interventions may be compromised by the effect of pedestrian movement.
1) signage interventions for stair use at work are not effective, and 2) signage interventions for stairs are not effective when pedestrian movement is controlled for in analyses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of stairs in office buildings.
the health of employees and their families.
the use of stairs in the context of a workplace.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
signage interventions for workplace climbing have limited effect.
there are more than 700, 000 reasons for caution when using signage interventions for stair use at work.
signage interventions for workplace stairs are unlikely to be effective in reducing cardiovascular disease risk.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
stair use is a function of the number of pedestrians at the stair/elevator choice-point, not the signage intervention.
the effects of signage intervention for stair climbing at the workplace is limited.
signage interventions to encourage stair climbing at work are not a reliable population health strategy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
signage interventions are not likely to be an effective strategy for encouraging stair climbing in the workplace.
the influence of pedestrian traffic on stair/elevator use is so great that it is impossible to discern effects of signage interventions.
signage interventions for workplace health are likely to be less effective than previously thought.
